items.text: Here's a number worth sitting with. The typical American homeowner has a net worth of around four hundred thousand dollars. The typical renter? About ten thousand. Same country, same economy — and a forty-to-one gap that mostly isn't salary. It's the house. For a middle-class family the home is usually the largest thing they will ever own, and a mortgage is how most people get there without the cash to buy outright. It turns a monthly payment into equity instead of a receipt.

It's also the largest debt most people ever take on, and the largest debt in the country. Mortgage balances run to almost thirteen trillion dollars — about three of every four dollars American households owe. Millions more get written every year, more than two trillion dollars' worth. That much money riding on a single loan, secured by the roof over somebody's head, is why so much care goes into how each one is built. In the two thousands that care broke down, and loose lending and a cascade of foreclosures nearly took the financial system with it. That's why mortgage originators have to be licensed today, and it's part of why this course exists. One more thing before you start. About fifty-three percent of people pass the licensing exam on their first attempt. On later attempts the rate is lower — closer to forty-seven percent. So the people retaking it are not, on the whole, finding it easier the second time around. That's the reason this app keeps asking you to produce answers instead of just read them.

A loan this large only works if the money reliably comes back. Hand somebody three hundred thousand dollars and a promise isn't enough — you need a way to enforce repayment, and a way to recover the money if the payments stop. The word itself is grim about this. Mortgage comes from the Old French for death pledge, and the pledge dies one of two ways: the borrower pays it off, or the borrower falls behind and loses the house that secures it. So a home loan is a promise to repay, secured by the house itself. And the promise and the claim on the house are two separate documents. Two. That split is the whole first section, and it trips up more new originators than anything else in this module.

The first document is the promissory note — the borrower's personal, written promise to repay. It spells out the amount borrowed, the interest rate, the monthly payment, and the term. The note is the debt. Once you sign it, you owe the money, full stop. But a note on its own is only a promise. It's an I-O-U. If that were all the lender had, a borrower who stopped paying could be chased like any other unpaid debt — a collections matter, a lawsuit, a judgment — and the lender would have no special claim on the house at all.

The second document fixes that. The mortgage — or, in many states, the deed of trust — is the security instrument. It pledges the property as collateral and creates a lien in the lender's favor: a legal claim attached to the home. That claim is what makes the loan secured. Worth noticing which word is which here, because everyday speech has it backwards. People say they're paying their mortgage when they mean they're paying the note. The mortgage is the lien. The note is the debt.

A mortgage is a two-party document — borrower and lender. A deed of trust does the same job but adds a neutral third party called the trustee, who holds title and can sell the property on default. Three parties instead of two. Which one your state uses matters more than it sounds. Deed-of-trust states can usually foreclose without going to court, which takes months. Mortgage states generally have to sue, and that can take years.

Because the lien exists, the lender has a remedy the note alone could never give: foreclosure, the legal process of enforcing the lien by forcing a sale to recover the unpaid debt. When more than one lien sits on the same property, lien position decides who gets paid out of that sale, and priority generally follows recording order. Whoever recorded first gets paid first. The main home loan is usually the first lien; a second mortgage or a home-equity line sits behind it. One exception is worth memorizing right now, because it comes back in later modules: unpaid property-tax liens typically jump ahead of even a first mortgage. The government gets paid before the bank does.
